newsitem.title: ZIMBABWE: Zimbabwe sugar output could double by 2002.
newsitem.headline: Zimbabwe sugar output could double by 2002.

text.p: Zimbabwe's annual sugar output is expected to more than double to 1.2 million tonnes in the next seven years if a number of planned expansion schemes are realised, local industry sources said this week.

Although officials of the southern African state's two main sugar producers declined to give details, the sources said both Triangle Limited and Hippo Valley were set to increase their output significantly because of plans to build a huge dam for irrigation water.
Hippo Valley and Triangle produce around 95 percent of the country's average 500,000-tonne annual sugar crop.

Earlier this month, the two companies signed an agreement with President Robert Mugabe's government to jointly build the country's largest dam, Tokwe-Mukorsi, for their sugar estates in southeastern Chiredzi lowveld.

Hippo and Triangle will have rights to 60 percent of the water from Tokwe-Mukorsi and the government 40 percent, in a deal that represents the percentages the two parties are investing in the dam which is expected to cost Z$390 million (U.S.$35.6 million).
Construction of the 1,751 billion cubic metre dam is scheduled to start between April and May, with completion set for 1999, according to Lands and Water Resources Minister Kumbirai Kangai.
But some economic analysts doubt Mugabe's cash-strapped government has the money to start the project in time.

Ezra Kanganga, public relations manager for Anglo American Corporation Zimbabwe which owns Hippo Valley, told Reuters the new dam would enhance Hippo's water security and lessen the risk of a serious drought severely affecting its production.
"The additional secured (water) will allow Hippo Valley to develop some new cane areas, which will allow sugar production to be increased," he said, giving no further details.
"The details of development work to be undertaken by Hippo Valley remain to be investigated. Until that is completed it is not possible to provide more precise information," Kanganga said.
But a senior industry official, who declined to be named, said the two firms' expansion programmes should see Zimbabwe's sugar production rising to above 1.2 million tonnes by around 2002.
"That's the sort of projection many are working around, and the fact that some of the current dams are filling up or rising significantly will help towards this realisation," he said.
One irrigation water source, Lake Mutirikwe, has risen to over 45 percent after two successive heavy rainy seasons, from just four percent at the start of the 1995/96 (November-April) wet season.
Mutirikwe's current water level provides Zimbabwe's lowveld sugar industry with a three-year water storage cover.
Another industry source said Triangle and Hippo Valley could, with the Tokwe-Mukorsi dam, expand their 25,000 hectares of sugar cane estates by 8,500 hectares in 1999.
Zimbabwe's sugar production is expected to rise to over 600,000 tonnes this year from 513,000 tonnes in 1996.
